slides.heading: Where did it begin?
slides.lead: The Great Fire of London began in a bakery in Pudding Lane in 1666. Say the name.

figure.shows: Historical reconstruction of the bakery on Pudding Lane where the Great Fire began
figure.subject: named

slides.heading: Why did wooden houses burn?
slides.lead: Many London houses had wooden parts. Look.

figure.shows: Historical reconstruction showing fire passing between closely spaced timber houses in London in 1666
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Strong winds spread fire
slides.lead: Strong winds blew sparks from the fire. These sparks could start new fires on other houses. Look.

figure.shows: Historical reconstruction of strong winds blowing glowing sparks from burning London houses towards other houses
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: How did strong winds help the fire spread?

options.why: Confuses wind with rain and does not recognise that the wind carried burning sparks.
Applies experience of blowing out a candle to a large fire in strong winds.

slides.heading: Fighting fire with water
slides.lead: People carried water in buckets and threw it onto flames. Water could put out small fires. Describe their action.

figure.shows: Historical reconstruction of Londoners using leather water buckets to fight a small fire in 1666
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Pulling down houses
slides.lead: People pulled down houses to make gaps. With no house to burn, fire could not easily cross. Explain why.

figure.shows: Historical reconstruction of Londoners pulling down a timber house to leave a broad gap between burning and unburnt houses
figure.subject: generic

myth.claim: People used modern fire engines in London in 1666.
myth.fact: People used water buckets and pulled down houses instead.

proof.line: A leather bucket carried water to the fire.

items.question: Explain how throwing water from buckets helped fight the fire.
items.answer: Water could put out small fires.

items.question: Explain how pulling down houses helped stop the fire spreading.
items.answer: Pulling down houses made gaps, so the fire had fewer houses to burn.

picture.shows: An imagined street of closely spaced wooden houses, one burning, with strong wind blowing sparks along the street
picture.subject: generic

items.question: Suppose wooden houses stand together in strong winds. Explain why fire could spread quickly.
items.answer: Wood can catch fire, and strong winds can blow sparks onto nearby houses.

items.question: Suppose water buckets cannot reach flames. Suggest another action to protect nearby wooden houses.
items.answer: Pull down houses to make a gap that the fire cannot easily cross.
